member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Streamline.IStreamlineGraphicsAdapter
member.summary: What Streamline needs of a backend that the RHI does not say: the native side of a session.

remarks.para: Small on purpose. Everything a session decides -- which features run, what options and constants are sent, which frame a call belongs to, how failures are reported -- is 's, once, for every API. A backend answers only the questions whose answers are native handles or native synchronisation, so a second API is a second adapter and nothing more.

Evaluation happens between passes, never inside one: the RHI's encoders open each pass as an object of their own and bind everything that pass uses when it opens, so no pipeline or descriptor state survives across Streamline's work for it to disturb. That is what lets a session run with Streamline's own state tracking switched off on either API.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Streamline.SignedModule
member.summary: Checks that a native module carries a valid Authenticode signature.

remarks.para: Streamline loads its plugins by name from a directory, which is a path this game does not own: the DLLs are fetched rather than built, and they sit beside the executable where anything can replace them. NVIDIA's own guidance is blunt about the consequence — a substituted plugin runs inside the process with the process's privileges — and the SDK ships sl::security::verifyEmbeddedSignature for exactly this. That helper is C++, so the same check is made here through the API it wraps.

This verifies the signature cryptographically and walks the certificate chain, then requires the signer to be NVIDIA — a merely valid signature would let anything with a code-signing certificate through, which is most of the threat. Revocation is checked only against what the machine has already cached, because a player launching a game offline should not be stalled on a network timeout to load an upscaler.

The SDK's own helper goes further: it applies a strong-signature crypto policy and additionally requires a second, NVIDIA-specific signature alongside the first. That is not reproduced here. The launcher's hash-checked install (or the fetch script, on a development checkout) is the trusted path onto disk, and this exists to catch a file that was replaced afterwards.

The first file that failed, with the reason, when one did.
member.returns: when every module in the folder is NVIDIA-signed.
member.remarks: The interposer alone is not enough. It loads its plugins by name from its own folder, and the plugins load the NGX models the same way, so one replaced sl.dlss.dll beside a genuine interposer runs in the game's process exactly as a replaced interposer would. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Streamline.SlApi
member.summary: The flat C entry points sl.interposer.dll exports, bound by address.

remarks.para: Bound with from a handle loaded by absolute path rather than declared with DllImport: the interposer lives in a folder the launcher chose, never beside the executable, and an import resolver can be registered only once per assembly — a second Vulkan device after an F10 switch would have had nowhere to put its own.

Every parameter is a raw pointer. Streamline's signatures take C++ references, which are pointers, and being explicit about that removes any question of what the marshaller decided to do — these calls sit on the render thread and the structures they point at have to stay put for the duration.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Streamline.SlAbi
member.summary: The Streamline SDK's own types, mirrored for P/Invoke.

remarks.para: Streamline's headers are C++ — namespaces, member functions, default arguments and a polymorphic frame token — but every function this backend needs is a flat extern "C" export on sl.interposer.dll or a feature function fetched by name, and every structure crossing that boundary is plain data. So the types are mirrored here rather than reached through a native shim: it keeps the repository free of C++, which matters because nothing else in it is native and the CI matrix builds on machines with no MSVC at all.

The price is that the layouts have to be exactly right, and a wrong one does not fail loudly — it hands the plugin a garbage pointer. The layouts below were therefore taken from the compiler rather than derived by hand: a throwaway program compiled against the 2.14.1 headers printed every sizeof, offsetof and the enum values that matter, and StreamlineLayoutTests pins those numbers. Change a field here and that test is what tells you.

Two traps are worth naming because a reasonable guess gets both wrong. structVersion is a size_t, so eight bytes and not four; a uint there shifts every field after it. And Boolean is enum Boolean : char — one byte, with a third value that means "not supplied", which is what several fields default to.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Streamline.StreamlineRuntime
member.summary: Owns one Streamline session: from slInit before the device to slShutdown before the device dies.

remarks.para: This must be constructed before the device. On Vulkan Streamline's documentation is explicit that the instance and device have to be created after slInit, and the reason is visible in what it does with them: in proxy mode its own vkCreateInstance and vkCreateDevice add the extensions, feature bits and extra queues its plugins need, so a device created first is one it cannot use, and the failure shows up later as a feature that simply reports itself unsupported. On Direct3D 12 the device comes from the Agility SDK's device factory, which the interposer cannot stand in for, so the session runs with manual hooking: the backend hands the device over with slSetD3DDevice and upgrades its DXGI factory so the swapchain is Streamline's to hook.
And it must be shut down before the device is destroyed: shutting down tears NGX down against that device, and doing it afterwards faults inside the driver with nothing in the log.
Every failure here is survivable. Each is reported once and leaves the caller with no runtime, and the backend runs its own temporal resolve exactly as it would have without one.

remarks.para: A frame here means a frame that reaches the screen, which is not the same as a pass of the host's loop. remarks.para: Everything here is the same on Vulkan and on Direct3D 12: which features run, the options and constants, Reflex, frame generation's state, and which frame every call belongs to. What Streamline needs that the RHI does not say -- the native image, its view, its format, the state it is in, the command list -- is asked of the backend through , so nothing above the backend ever holds a native handle and no backend repeats any of this.

Evaluation happens between passes, never inside one: the encoder opens each pass as an object of its own and binds everything that pass uses when it opens, so no pipeline or descriptor state survives across Streamline's work for it to disturb. A full barrier either side makes what was written before visible to Streamline and what Streamline wrote visible after. That is what lets the session run with Streamline's own state tracking switched off.
